title: MYP Physical and Health Education Criteria A-D
summary: MYP Physical and Health Education criteria A-D explained for students and parents, with plain-language feedback examples and high-band expectations.
body_markdown:
The **MYP Physical and Health Education criteria** assess four connected abilities: understanding PHE concepts, planning improvement, performing effectively, and reflecting on performance. Each criterion is assessed on a 0-8 scale, with descriptors that change across MYP year levels. Strong athletic ability alone does not demonstrate achievement across all four criteria.


Imagine a student opening an assignment and finding “justify your plan” beside their mark. The score is clear; the next step feels less obvious. Understanding the criteria turns that feedback into practical guidance. This guide explains each criterion, illustrates stronger responses, and helps students and parents interpret teacher comments. Always use your school’s year-specific rubric and task instructions.


### The MYP PHE criteria at a glance


The four criteria are equally weighted in the subject framework. Together, they assess more than sporting ability.


Criterion Plain-language question Typical evidence


A: Knowing and understanding Can you explain and apply relevant ideas? Explanations, analysis and accurate terminology


B: Planning for performance Can you design and evaluate an improvement plan? Goals, activities, justification and outcome analysis


C: Applying and performing Can you apply skills and strategies effectively? Technique, tactics, decisions and adaptation


D: Reflecting and improving performance Can you evaluate performance and improve? Evidence, interpersonal skills and improvement strategies


Explore the[MYP PHE objectives and skills](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/physical-and-health-education-objectives-and-skills-in-myp) for subject context, or compare PHE with the[eight MYP subject groups](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-subjects-are-taught-in-myp) .


A student searches a feedback sheet with an oversized magnifying glass while another suggests reading the feedback


### Criterion A: Knowing and understanding


A teacher might write: *“You identified the fitness components, but explain how they affect performance.”*


Criterion A asks students to use factual, procedural and conceptual knowledge. Defining a term provides a starting point. Stronger responses explain relationships, apply knowledge to the task and communicate using accurate PHE terminology.


For cardiovascular endurance in football, a student could explain how it supports sustained movement, connect that demand to a playing position, and use the connection to recommend suitable training.


High-band work generally:


- explains relevant ideas accurately and thoroughly
- applies knowledge to the particular performer or situation
- connects concepts through clear reasoning
- uses terminology accurately and effectively


The useful question is: “Have I explained how and why?” RevisionDojo’s Study Notes can support understanding, Flashcards can reinforce terminology, and the Questionbank can support application practice. The[MYP study resources guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-myp-study-guides-by-subject) explains how to combine resources purposefully.


### Criterion B: Planning for performance


Another comment might read: *“Your sessions are clear, but explain why they support your goal.”*


Criterion B concerns designing a plan to improve physical performance or health and examining its effectiveness. Expectations develop across MYP years, so students should check which planning, explanation and evaluation strands their task assesses.


“Do cone drills twice a week” identifies an activity. A stronger agility plan establishes a starting point, sets a measurable goal, chooses suitable drills and explains progression. Each decision should connect to the performer’s needs.


A useful planning checklist includes:


- baseline evidence and a focused improvement goal
- appropriate activities, frequency, intensity and progression
- reasoning that connects training choices to the goal
- safe, realistic sessions and a way to monitor results
- outcome analysis where required by the rubric


When evaluating, compare initial and final evidence. Explain what contributed to the outcome, acknowledge limitations and propose specific changes. Improvement alone does not explain why a plan worked.


### Criterion C: Applying and performing


Practical feedback might say: *“Your passing was controlled during drills, but became inconsistent under pressure.”*


Criterion C assesses skills, techniques, strategies and information applied during performance. The relevant evidence depends on the unit: a dance routine, team game and fitness activity require different demonstrations.


An accurate unopposed pass shows technique. A game also requires scanning, selecting a receiver, adjusting force and timing, and responding to opponents. Strong performance brings execution and decision-making together.


High-band evidence commonly includes controlled execution, effective movement concepts, appropriate tactics and decisions that respond to changing conditions. Students may also need to analyse and apply information during performance.


Read the task-specific clarification before practising. Identify the assessed skill, the conditions in which it must appear and how the teacher will observe it. Then practise under conditions that resemble the assessment, with appropriate supervision and safety measures.


### Criterion D: Reflecting and improving performance


A final comment might read: *“You described what happened. Evaluate why it happened and identify your next step.”*


Criterion D connects reflection with improvement. Depending on the year-level descriptors, it includes interpersonal skills, goals, strategies, and analysis and evaluation of performance.


“My communication was poor” is too broad to guide action. A stronger reflection identifies late defensive calls, explains their effect on team positioning and proposes an agreed call before the next transition.


Use a simple sequence: identify specific evidence, analyse its meaning, judge strengths and limitations, and select a realistic improvement strategy. Later, check whether that strategy helped.


RevisionDojo’s AI Chat can help students question vague reasoning, while Grading tools can support reviewing explanations. Students should retain ownership of their reflection and check suggestions against teacher guidance.


### Turn feedback into your next action


Start with one teacher comment. Identify the criterion and command term, then locate the missing evidence. Revise a paragraph, training decision or performance goal before transferring that lesson to the next task.


The[guide to MYP Criteria A, B, C and D](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-criteria-a-b-c-d-explained) and[MYP criteria by subject](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-criteria-per-subject) explain why familiar letters have different meanings across subjects.


Before submission, translate each assessed strand into a question and check where your evidence answers it. Parents can support this process by asking students to explain their reasoning.
